cemc-fryer-2014-01a.title: Count by number of digits
cemc-fryer-2014-01a.body:
$1$–$9$: $9$ one-digit numbers give $9$ digits. $10$–$99$: $90$ two-digit numbers give $180$ digits. Total $189$.

**Answer: 189**

cemc-fryer-2014-01a.title: Pretend all are two-digit
cemc-fryer-2014-01a.body:
Write $1$–$9$ as $01$–$09$: then all $99$ numbers have two digits, $198$ digits in total. Remove the $9$ extra leading zeros: $198 - 9 = 189$.

**Answer: 189**

cemc-fryer-2014-01b.title: Add the three-digit numbers
cemc-fryer-2014-01b.body:
From part (a), $1$–$99$ give $189$ digits. The $100$ numbers $100$–$199$ give $300$ more. Total $489$.

**Answer: 489**

cemc-fryer-2014-01c.title: Continue past 199
cemc-fryer-2014-01c.body:
From part (b), $1$–$199$ give $489$ digits. We need $1155 - 489 = 666$ more, i.e. $666 \div 3 = 222$ more three-digit numbers: $200, \dots, 421$. So $n = 421$.

**Answer: 421**

cemc-fryer-2014-01c.title: Formula
cemc-fryer-2014-01c.body:
For a three-digit $n$, the number of digits is $9 + 180 + 3(n - 99) = 3n - 108$. Setting $3n - 108 = 1155$ gives $n = 421$.

**Answer: 421**

cemc-fryer-2014-01d.title: Locate the digit
cemc-fryer-2014-01d.body:
From part (c), $1$–$421$ use $1155$ digits. We need $1358 - 1155 = 203$ more. Since $203 = 3 \times 67 + 2$, the next $67$ numbers ($422$–$488$) use $201$ digits, and the 1358th digit is the 2nd digit of $489$, which is $8$.

**Answer: 8**

cemc-fryer-2014-01d.title: Use the formula
cemc-fryer-2014-01d.body:
Up to a three-digit $n$ there are $3n - 108$ digits. Up to $488$: $3(488) - 108 = 1356$ digits. So digits 1357, 1358, 1359 are the digits $4, 8, 9$ of $489$. The 1358th is $8$.

**Answer: 8**

cemc-fryer-2014-02a.title: Exterior angle
cemc-fryer-2014-02a.body:
Extend $BC$ past $C$. The exterior angle at $C$ is $180^\circ - 50^\circ = 130^\circ$, and it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: $60^\circ + \angle BAC$. So $\angle BAC = 70^\circ$.

**Answer: 70°**

cemc-fryer-2014-02b.title: Use angle A
cemc-fryer-2014-02b.body:
$\angle DBC + \angle DCB = \frac12(\angle B + \angle C) = \frac12(180^\circ - \angle A) = 90^\circ - \frac12 \angle A$. So $\angle BDC = 90^\circ + \frac12 \angle A = 90^\circ + 35^\circ = 125^\circ$.

**Answer: 125°**

cemc-fryer-2014-02c.title: Isosceles triangle
cemc-fryer-2014-02c.body:
$\triangle SQR$ is isosceles ($QS = RS$), so $\angle SQR = \angle SRQ = x$, and $2x + 140^\circ = 180^\circ$ gives $x = 20^\circ$.

The bisectors double these: $\angle PQR = \angle PRQ = 40^\circ$. So $\angle QPR = 180^\circ - 80^\circ = 100^\circ$.

**Answer: 100°**

cemc-fryer-2014-02c.title: Use the formula from (b)
cemc-fryer-2014-02c.body:
As in part (b), for angle bisectors from $Q$ and $R$ meeting at $S$: $\angle QSR = 90^\circ + \frac12 \angle QPR$. So $140^\circ = 90^\circ + \frac12 \angle QPR$, giving $\angle QPR = 100^\circ$. (Here $QS = RS$ isn't even needed.)

**Answer: 100°**

cemc-fryer-2014-02d.title: Assume it and find a contradiction
cemc-fryer-2014-02d.body:
Suppose $\angle QSR = 80^\circ$. In isosceles $\triangle SQR$, $\angle SQR = \angle SRQ = \frac{180^\circ - 80^\circ}{2} = 50^\circ$. Then $\angle PQR = \angle PRQ = 100^\circ$, and $\angle QPR = 180^\circ - 200^\circ = -20^\circ$, which is impossible.

So $\angle QSR$ cannot be $80^\circ$.

cemc-fryer-2014-02d.title: The angle is always obtuse
cemc-fryer-2014-02d.body:
For any triangle, $\angle SQR + \angle SRQ = \frac12(\angle PQR + \angle PRQ) < \frac12 \cdot 180^\circ = 90^\circ$. Hence
$$\angle QSR = 180^\circ - (\angle SQR + \angle SRQ) > 90^\circ.$$
So $\angle QSR$ can never be $80^\circ$.

cemc-fryer-2014-03a.title: Base and height
cemc-fryer-2014-03a.body:
Base $BC = 10$ along the $x$-axis, height $= $ the $y$-coordinate of $A$, $9$. Area $= \frac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 = 45$.

**Answer: 45**

cemc-fryer-2014-03a.title: Half a rectangle
cemc-fryer-2014-03a.body:
The triangle has base $10$ and fits in a $10 \times 9$ rectangle with its apex on the top side, so its area is half the rectangle: $\frac12 \cdot 90 = 45$.

**Answer: 45**

cemc-fryer-2014-03b.title: Check Dexter's options
cemc-fryer-2014-03b.body:
The base stays $10$, so the area is $25$ exactly when $A$ has $y$-coordinate $5$. The winner is whoever moves $A$ down to $y = 5$.

- If Dexter moves down to $(2, 6)$, Ella moves down to $(2, 5)$ and wins.
- If Dexter moves left to $(1, 7)$, Ella moves left to $(0, 7)$. Now Dexter cannot move left, so he must move down to $(0, 6)$, and Ella moves down to $(0, 5)$ and wins.

Either way Ella wins.

cemc-fryer-2014-03b.title: Copy Dexter
cemc-fryer-2014-03b.body: Ella can simply repeat Dexter's move each time. From $(2, 7)$ both "distances" — $2$ steps left available, $2$ steps down to $y = 5$ — are even. After each pair of moves (Dexter's then Ella's) both stay even, so Dexter can never be the one to reach $y = 5$ (he would need an odd distance of $1$), and he can never leave Ella without a copying move (a left move by Dexter leaves an odd number of left steps, at least $1$, for Ella). Eventually Ella makes the move to $y = 5$.

cemc-fryer-2014-03ci.title: Mirror strategy
cemc-fryer-2014-03ci.body:
The second player, **Geoff**, has a winning strategy: always make the same move (left or down) that Faisal just made. See part (ii)/(iii) for why it works.

**Answer: Geoff**

cemc-fryer-2014-03ci.title: Parity view
cemc-fryer-2014-03ci.body:
From $(6, 9)$, there are $6$ possible left moves and $4$ down moves until $y = 5$ — both even. Whenever both numbers are even, the player to move (Faisal) leaves an odd number in one of them, and the opponent can restore evenness. The player who restores $y - 5$ to $0$ wins, and that is always the second player.

**Answer: Geoff**

cemc-fryer-2014-03cii.title: Copy every move
cemc-fryer-2014-03cii.body:
**Strategy:** on each turn, Geoff makes the same move (left or down) that Faisal just made.

**Geoff can always copy.**
- *Left moves:* $x$ starts at $6$ (even). After Faisal moves left, $x$ is odd, hence at least $1$, so Geoff can also move left, making $x$ even again. So after each of Geoff's turns, $x$ is even.
- *Down moves:* $y$ starts at $9$. Down moves come in pairs (Faisal, then Geoff), so after Geoff's turns $y$ is $9, 7, 5$, ... and after Faisal's turns $y$ is $8, 6$. The game ends when $y = 5$, before $y$ could go negative.

**Geoff wins.** The area is $25$ exactly when $y = 5$ (base $10$, height $5$). Since Faisal always faces an odd $y$ ($9$ or $7$) and moves it to an even value ($8$ or $6$), Faisal can never make $y = 5$. Geoff copies down moves, so he moves $y$ from $6$ to $5$ and wins. (Left moves cannot go on forever, since $x \ge 0$; once $x = 0$ only down moves remain.) ∎

cemc-fryer-2014-04a.title: Build from A
cemc-fryer-2014-04a.body: Each subset of $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is a subset of $\{1, 2\}$, with or without $3$. The subset sums of $\{1, 2\}$ are $0, 1, 2, 3$; adding $3$ gives $3, 4, 5, 6$. So the eight sums are $0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6$.

cemc-fryer-2014-04b.title: Each element appears in half the subsets
cemc-fryer-2014-04b.body:
There are $2^5 = 32$ subsets. Each element is in exactly $2^4 = 16$ of them (it is included; each of the other four elements is in or out). So each element contributes $16$ times its value, and the total is
$$16(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5) = 16 \times 15 = 240.$$

**Answer: 240**

cemc-fryer-2014-04b.title: Pair complements
cemc-fryer-2014-04b.body:
Pair each subset with its complement. The two subset sums in each pair add to $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$. There are $32 / 2 = 16$ pairs, so the total is $16 \times 15 = 240$.

**Answer: 240**

cemc-fryer-2014-04c.title: Odd part and multiple-of-4 part
cemc-fryer-2014-04c.body:
Split each subset into its odd part $O \subseteq \{1, 3, 5, 7\}$ and its part $M \subseteq \{4, 8, 12, 16\}$. The sum of $M$ is always a multiple of $4$, so the subset sum is divisible by $4$ exactly when the sum of $O$ is.

The subsets of $\{1, 3, 5, 7\}$ with sum divisible by $4$: $\{\}$ (0), $\{1, 3\}$ (4), $\{1, 7\}$ (8), $\{3, 5\}$ (8), $\{5, 7\}$ (12), $\{1, 3, 5, 7\}$ (16). (Odd-size subsets have odd sums, and $\{1, 5\}$, $\{3, 7\}$ give $6$, $10$.)

As in part (b), the $16$ subsets $M$ have sums totalling $8(4 + 8 + 12 + 16) = 320$. For a fixed good $O$ with sum $s$, the $16$ subsets $O \cup M$ have sums totalling $16s + 320$:
$$320 + 384 + 448 + 448 + 512 + 576 = 2688.$$

**Answer: 2688**

cemc-fryer-2014-04c.title: Count contributions
cemc-fryer-2014-04c.body:
Every good subset is $O \cup M$ with one of the $6$ good odd parts $O$ and any of the $16$ parts $M$. Adding up all their sums:
- each good $O$ appears with $16$ choices of $M$, contributing $16 \times (0 + 4 + 8 + 8 + 12 + 16) = 16 \times 48 = 768$;
- each $M$ appears with $6$ choices of $O$, contributing $6 \times 320 = 1920$.

Total: $768 + 1920 = 2688$.

**Answer: 2688**
